defaults.permitted_development: Detached outbuildings such as sheds, workshops and garages can usually be permitted development in Wales where they remain incidental to the house, stay within the curtilage, are not placed forward of the principal elevation and meet the Welsh siting and height limits. That route does not cover separate self-contained living accommodation.

rules.height_rules: Maximum height is 4m for a dual-pitched roof, 3m for a single-pitch or other roof form and 2.5m for a flat roof. Eaves should not exceed 2.5m, and any part within 2m of a boundary should not exceed 2.5m in height.
rules.depth_rules: There is no standalone depth allowance. The key tests are whether the building stays within the curtilage, remains behind the principal elevation and keeps the total area covered by outbuildings and other additions within 50% of the curtilage excluding the original house.
rules.boundary_rules: Outbuildings cannot be placed forward of the principal elevation and cannot extend beyond the side elevation where that would bring them closer to a highway than the house, or within 5m of the highway, whichever is nearer. Any part within 2m of a boundary should stay at or below 2.5m, and any part within 2m of the house should stay at or below 1.5m.
rules.roof_rules: Outbuildings should remain single storey. Roof form controls the allowed height directly, and verandas, balconies or raised platforms projecting more than 300mm above ground level are not permitted under the normal Welsh outbuilding right.
rules.materials_rules: The building should remain clearly subordinate to the house, use finishes that sit comfortably with the dwelling and not be laid out or used as separate self-contained accommodation.

rules.permitted_development: Welsh permitted development can often cover a detached garage, shed or similar garden building, but only while it remains incidental to the house, sits in the right part of the plot and stays within the national size and height rules. Self-contained living use falls outside that route.

rules.height_rules: The usual Welsh limit is a single-storey building with eaves no higher than 2.5m, a 4m maximum for a roof with more than one pitch, a 3m maximum for other pitched forms and a 2.5m maximum for a flat roof. Anything within 2m of a boundary should stay at or below 2.5m overall.
rules.depth_rules: Rather than a fixed projection limit, Welsh outbuilding rules focus on curtilage position, not building forward of the principal elevation and keeping overall site coverage by additions and outbuildings within the normal 50% allowance.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary and highway siting are crucial in Wales. The building should stay behind the principal elevation, avoid side positions that bring it nearer to the highway than the house or within 5m of it, stay within 2.5m overall if within 2m of a boundary and stay within 1.5m high if any part is within 2m of the house.
rules.roof_rules: Keep the roof simple and the building single storey. Dual-pitched roofs can use the higher 4m cap, other roof forms less, and any veranda, balcony or raised platform above 300mm would need a fuller planning assessment.
rules.materials_rules: A Welsh outbuilding can use modern or traditional finishes, but it should still look subordinate to the house and remain incidental in use rather than drifting into self-contained accommodation.

restrictions.listed_building: Listed building consent may be needed for internal or external works that affect the character of a listed building or its curtilage structures. Minor-looking changes can still need consent in Wales.
restrictions.article4_notes: No borough-wide Article 4 note is recorded here, but site-specific directions or planning conditions can still remove permitted development rights on particular properties.

rules.permitted_development: In Wales, an outbuilding can often use householder permitted development rights if it stays incidental to the enjoyment of the house, remains behind the principal elevation and complies with the national curtilage, coverage and height limits. It should not operate as a separate dwelling or annexe.

rules.height_rules: Use the Welsh height limits: up to 4m overall with more than one roof pitch, up to 3m with a single-pitch or other roof form, and up to 2.5m with a flat roof. Eaves should stay at or below 2.5m, and boundary siting within 2m also brings a 2.5m cap.
rules.depth_rules: Outbuildings in Wales are not controlled by a separate depth figure. What matters is curtilage location, staying behind the principal elevation and not pushing total coverage by additions and outbuildings beyond 50% of the curtilage apart from the original house.
rules.boundary_rules: The Welsh siting rules are often the hardest part: keep the building behind the principal elevation, do not push it past the side elevation in a way that comes closer to the highway than the house or within 5m of it, limit anything within 2m of a boundary to 2.5m overall and keep any part within 2m of the house to 1.5m high.
rules.roof_rules: The permitted Welsh form is a modest single-storey building. The roof type determines the height cap, and balconies, verandas or raised platforms above 300mm fall outside the ordinary outbuilding route.
rules.materials_rules: Materials should help the building read as an ancillary domestic structure rather than a second dwelling. Even with modern finishes, it should stay subordinate to the house and not operate as self-contained living space.
